analysis: A Liverpool creamware jug with a black transfer portrait of COMMODORE PREBLE in an oval cartouche, Fame blowing a trumpet above, an allegorical figure with the American flag and shield below. Edward Preble was born in Falmouth -- now Portland -- in 1761 and commanded the Mediterranean squadron against Tripoli in 1803-04; he is Maine's naval hero, and a period Liverpool jug bearing his portrait is about as directly on this collection's Maine criterion as a ceramic can get. The object itself reads right: warm cream body, a fine engraved period transfer, all-over crazing, and the pear form with strap handle that belongs to c.1805-1815. Estimated $400-600, which is inside the band with room, and that estimate exists because of the damage.
problems: There is real condition loss and it is the whole reason this is affordable. A chip with staining at the rim just left of the spout, a chip at the foot rim, scattered dark specks and what may be an old repair line running down the spout. That is exactly the condition-discount case the collecting brief describes: the market punishes a chipped rim far out of proportion to how it looks on a shelf, and a jug like this at full condition is $1,500-3,000. Verify at preview that the spout is not restored -- restoration on creamware fluoresces under UV -- and that the transfer has not been strengthened. American-subject Liverpool jugs are also reproduced, but the reproductions are hard-bodied and too white; this is not one.
patience: Low to moderate. American naval Liverpool jugs run periodically, but Preble specifically -- the one that matters in Maine -- is uncommon and will be wanted in this room.

analysis: An 1793 memorial to Elizabeth Titcomb of Newburyport, Massachusetts, $600-800. Dated to the year and named to the individual and the town, which is the best documentation any needlework can carry. Mourning and memorial pieces from the Federal-period New England female academies are a serious collecting field, and Newburyport is a documented centre. Two hundred and thirty-three years old, catalogued to the year, and inside the band -- one of the few objects in this sale where age, documentation and price all line up.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in it sits at the top of the band. The frame is not original -- the description says 'in VINTAGE pressed brass, wavy glass and pine backboard', so the wavy glass and brass surround are a later, if sympathetic, housing. Condition is stated as 'toned, faded but legible', and on a calligraphic memorial legibility is the whole object. And the catalogue's genealogy does not hold: it gives Elizabeth (Starkey) Titcomb as 1758-1793 and then says she 'had a son named Beniah (1796-1876)' -- three years after her death, so the son is presumably by a second marriage. That kind of error gets repeated into a provenance if nobody checks it.
patience: Moderate. Dated Federal memorials appear a few times a year in New England sales.

analysis: A pair of 17th-century Spanish brass candlesticks, $500-700. Catalogued to the century, so on the house's own claim these are around 350 years old -- older than almost anything else in the sale that is inside the band. Spanish and Flemish brass of the period is heavy, hand-turned and cast, with pronounced tooling marks and a deep unpolished patina, and a surviving pair is considerably better than a single.
problems: Seventeenth-century brass is one of the most reproduced categories in decorative metalwork -- Victorian and 1920s Dutch and Spanish revival candlesticks copy the forms exactly and have themselves been aged for a century. The tells are the casting seams, the way the socket and stem are joined (period ones are pinned or threaded coarsely), file marks rather than lathe marks, and a patina that sits in the recesses. Confirm both are a true pair rather than a married one -- measure and weigh them.
patience: Moderate. Early brass runs periodically; catalogued 17th-century pairs inside this budget do not.

analysis: A 19th-century William Soutter & Sons copper tea kettle, $100-150 -- the cheapest lot in this whole section and one of very few that hits two criteria at once. Soutter of Birmingham is a documented maker, the date is catalogued to the century, and a marked English copper kettle with its original handle is an honest, useful object. Everything else in the copper category in this sale is undated and unmarked; this one is neither.
problems: Decorative copper is the weak market the standing brief names, and a kettle is a kettle. Check the base for a burn-through -- kettles used on ranges thin at the bottom -- and that the handle wrap and the finial are original. The maker's mark should be struck on the base; confirm it is there and legible rather than taken on trust.
patience: High. English copper kettles run constantly; marked and dated ones at $100 do not stay cheap by much.

analysis: A correction to my own earlier reading. I wrote that this was bone rather than ivory and that 'none of the marine-mammal or elephant restrictions apply'. The description says otherwise: it is a 'Miniature Semi-articulated Carved WHALE BONE Skeleton'. Whale bone is marine mammal material and squarely within the Marine Mammal Protection Act -- the distinction I drew between bone and ivory is the wrong distinction; the one that matters is whether the animal was a marine mammal. Everything else about the lot is as good as I said, and better: it sits in a carved walnut coffin on a bed of an 1808 farmer's ledger inscribed 'Public Burdens' and 'James Frier, Farmer at Brotherston', which is a genuinely charming piece of documentation.
problems: Whale bone, undocumented. Resale is zero for the same reason as every other marine-mammal lot in this sale: it cannot lawfully be sold on without proof of age and origin that does not accompany it. Also worth noting the catalogue's own note misspells the place -- it gives 'Brotherston' in the inscription and 'Brotherton' in the gloss.

analysis: A German plaster model of a mathematical abstract, circa 1900, $400-600. These are the Brill and Schilling teaching models -- plaster surfaces cast to illustrate algebraic geometry, made in Halle and Leipzig for university mathematics departments from the 1870s to about 1930. They are genuinely antique, genuinely scientific instruments of a kind, and they have a serious second audience among design collectors because Man Ray photographed them and the Surrealists adopted them. Catalogued to c.1900 and inside the band with room.
problems: Plaster is fragile and these chip at every edge; many surviving models have lost their thread inlays and their original numbered labels. Check for the impressed or printed catalogue number, which identifies which surface it is and is much of the value. Confirm it is a period Schilling or Brill model rather than a mid-20th-century university copy. A niche object with a small but real market.
patience: Low to moderate. Mathematical models surface irregularly and are usually deaccessioned in groups.

analysis: A pair of miniature Italian micromosaics of musical couples, $500-700. Roman micromosaic -- thousands of hand-drawn glass tesserae set in a mastic ground -- is a genuine and technically extraordinary craft, and Grand Tour micromosaics of the early to mid 19th century are collected on their own terms. A matched pair of figural panels is better than singles.
problems: No date. Micromosaic quality varies enormously with the tessera count -- the fine early Vatican-workshop pieces have hundreds per square centimetre, the late tourist ones have a fraction of that, and the difference is tenfold in price. Judge under magnification. Micromosaics also crack and lose tesserae, and the losses are usually filled with paint. At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band.
patience: Moderate. Grand Tour micromosaics appear regularly; good figural pairs less often.

analysis: The description dates this to within about a year, and by the best possible method -- counting the stars. 'Wool and Metallic Thread PERIOD Embroidery on polished cotton ground, depicting a spread wing eagle holding crossed arrows, flanked by AMERICAN 20-STAR FLAG (1817-1818) and the DUTCH FLAG, the riband at top reading "Je Main Tidrai" the official national motto of the Netherlands.' The twenty-star flag was official only from 4 July 1817 to 3 July 1818, so the object dates itself. And the subject is far more interesting than 'patriotic woolie' suggests: an American eagle paired with the Dutch flag and the House of Orange motto is a commemorative of the American-Dutch relationship, most likely tied to the trade and loan connections between the young republic and Amsterdam. That is a specific historical object, not generic patriotic needlework. It also partly rescues the terminology I criticised -- it genuinely is wool, though 'woolie' still properly means a British sailor's wool-on-wool ship picture.
problems: The ground is shattered and lost over roughly a third of the area -- it survives as a fragment on a mat, and that is why a dated 1817-18 embroidery is $300-500. Shattered silk-era textiles cannot be stabilised cheaply and will continue to degrade; frame it out of light and leave it alone. The riband is transcribed 'Je Main Tidrai' where the motto is 'Je Maintiendrai', so either the embroiderer or the cataloguer has garbled it -- worth reading yourself, because a phonetic misspelling by the maker would be evidence of an American rather than a Dutch hand.
patience: Low. Dated American patriotic needlework of the 1810s is genuinely scarce, even damaged.

analysis: An oval silver medal engraved with Washington and a Native American figure, inscribed GEORGE WASHINGTON PRESIDENT 1792, with an applied rim and suspension loop -- catalogued as a 1792 Washington Indian Peace Medal, small size, at $800-1,200. The estimate is the evidence. Genuine 1792 oval Washington peace medals are among the rarest objects in American numismatics; a handful survive and they sell in the hundreds of thousands of dollars. No auction house prices one at $800. Per the standing principle about estimates an order of magnitude below a genuine work, believe the estimate rather than the title.
problems: The photograph supports the reading: the engraving is soft and the surface granular, where genuine examples are crisply hand-engraved on rolled silver sheet. Reproductions and restrikes of these have been made since the 19th century, some of them old enough to be interesting in their own right. As silver it has a small melt floor, but no weight is given so none can be calculated. Do not bid this on the title.
patience: Not applicable -- the genuine article is not obtainable at any patience level in this budget.

analysis: Circa 1840 George Washington 'campaign' andirons, $600-800. Catalogued to the decade, genuinely antique, and figural cast-iron andirons of Washington are a documented American form associated with the 1840 Harrison campaign and the patriotic revival around it. A pair is much better than a single.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band. Figural andirons are reproduced heavily -- Virginia Metalcrafters and others cast Washington andirons through the 20th century, and old paint hides the difference. The tells are the casting quality, the sand texture on the reverse, and the shaft-to-billet joint. Confirm both match and that the billet bars are present.
patience: Moderate. Figural andirons run regularly; period Washingtons less often.

analysis: Two missionary mail covers, Canton to Siam and Canton to Bangkok, 1840 and 1841, $500-700. Dated to the year, genuinely antique, and pre-stamp China trade covers to Southeast Asia are legitimately scarce postal history -- the routes, the handstamps and the missionary correspondence networks are all documented and collected. This is the kind of narrow, well-evidenced material where scarcity is real rather than asserted.
problems: Postal history is a specialist market with specialist buyers who will be online for exactly this lot; the price will be found. At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band. Covers of this period are also faked and 'improved' -- added handstamps and made-up franking are standard. Condition and the completeness of the folded letter matter. Nothing in this connects to any of the buyer's five criteria beyond age.
patience: Low. Genuinely scarce, but also genuinely outside the collection's interests.

analysis: A mid-19th-century mahogany travelling apothecary case, $600-800. Catalogued to the period, genuinely antique, and a fitted apothecary or medicine chest with its bottles, drawer, scales and labels is one of the most satisfying objects of its kind -- a complete system in a box. These are also exactly the cased sets where the standing rule applies most sharply.
problems: Completeness is the entire question and it is the standing rule for cased sets: count the bottles against the fitted recesses, check the secret drawer is present and its contents, and see whether the original labels, glass stoppers and scale pans survive. A chest missing half its bottles is worth a third of a complete one. At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band, which assumes a good answer.
patience: Moderate. Apothecary chests run periodically; complete ones are the minority.

analysis: Two early English mocha ware mugs, $800-1,200. Mocha -- the dendritic, cat's-eye, earthworm and marbled slip decoration on creamware and pearlware -- is one of the genuinely serious collecting fields in English pottery, with a devoted American following, and early mugs are the heart of it. Comfortably antique. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Mocha is also reproduced, and the Don Carpentier and later studio revivals are excellent -- the tells are the body, the glaze pooling and the slip banding. Mugs are used objects; expect rim chips and hairlines, which on mocha are a substantial discount. No date beyond 'early'.
patience: Moderate. Mocha appears in most good English pottery sales.

analysis: Two early 19th-century English Staffordshire jugs, $800-1,200. Catalogued to the period and genuinely antique. Transfer-printed and lustre Staffordshire jugs of the 1810s-30s are abundant but the American-market and historical-subject ones are collected. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. No subjects named, which is the whole valuation on Staffordshire jugs -- an American historical or naval subject is worth several times a floral one. Compare 2294, the Preble jug, which is the same idea inside the band and with the subject named.
patience: High. Staffordshire jugs are deep supply.

analysis: The description answers the material question and it goes against the lot. Two sticks: 'Sailor made cane, with a WHALE'S TOOTH handle and tapered WHALE BONE shaft, 32 1/4" long; and Walking stick with an angled carved bone top decorated with a potted flower, wooden shaft'. The first is marine mammal twice over -- tooth and bone -- and it is the better of the two, a genuine sailor-made piece of exactly the kind this collection is drawn to. The second, plain carved bone on a wooden shaft, is unrestricted but ordinary.
problems: The sailor-made cane is whale's tooth and whale bone, undocumented, so the lot cannot be resold as offered and resale is recorded as zero. This reverses my earlier BUY IF CHEAP, which was written before the description was available and assumed unspecified carving.
patience: High. Cane lots run regularly at Thomaston.

analysis: A 19th-century lantern, $300-400. Catalogued to the century so genuinely antique, and a period tin or iron lantern -- barn, ship or candle -- is an honest object with real presence. Inside the band.
problems: Nothing about it is described: not the material, not the type, not the fuel, not the size, and a ship's lantern, a barn lantern and a candle lantern are three different markets. Lanterns are also the most reproduced 'primitive' after weathervanes. Original glass and an original burner are what matter and neither is mentioned.

analysis: A painted wooden 'Jersey' coffee bin, $300-500. Country-store bins with original stencilled or painted lettering are collected as advertising and as folk painting at once, and the surviving paint is the whole value. An appealing object with real graphic presence.
problems: No date. Store bins are reproduced for the decorator trade in exactly this form, and repainted originals are common -- the tells are wear that follows use (the lid edge, the front where hands went), paint that has crazed rather than been distressed, and old nail and hinge types. Check the interior, which is never repainted on a fake as carefully as the outside.

analysis: A 'Colonial style' eight-arm wood and iron chandelier, $300-500. 'Style' is the cataloguer declining to commit, and on a Colonial chandelier that means 20th-century Colonial Revival -- these were made in enormous numbers from the 1920s onward and are still made today.
problems: 'Style' with no date. Rewiring cost. Estimate is above the market for revival lighting.

analysis: An early 19th-century Pennsylvania Dutch pie safe, $1,000-1,500. Catalogued to the period and genuinely antique; punched-tin pie safes with good tin panels are collected as folk furniture and the Pennsylvania ones are the classic form. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget, and a large piece of country furniture. Pie safes are heavily reproduced and 'married' -- new carcases with old tins and old carcases with new tins are both common. Original paint and original tins matter enormously; check the tin nail holes against the frame and whether the punched patterns are consistent across all panels.
patience: High. Pie safes run regularly in Americana sales.

analysis: Two tri-ply bentwood and wire farmhouse sifters, $200-300. Honest kitchen bentwood -- steamed and lapped bands with wire mesh -- of a type made from the mid-19th century into the 20th. Cheap, characterful, and the kind of unfashionable object the collecting brief is built to find.
problems: No date, and bentwood sieves changed little over eighty years. Wire mesh rusts and tears; the bands split at the lap. Estimate is above the market -- these sell for $30-80 each. Buy well below.

analysis: An oblong tilt-top candlestand, $300-400. Small tilt-top stands are the most useful antique furniture form there is -- they take no space, they are genuinely usable, and period ones are affordable because the market for brown furniture has collapsed. An oblong rather than round top is a slightly less common variant.
problems: No date at all, which on a candlestand is the question -- Colonial Revival copies of these were made by the thousand from 1900 onward. Judge it underneath: hand-cut dovetails on the birdcage, irregular saw marks, shrinkage that has made the top oval, and old oxidation in the unfinished areas. Circular saw marks mean post-1830 at the earliest and usually much later. Check the tilt mechanism and the leg-to-shaft dovetails, which is where these break.
patience: Very high. Candlestands are in every sale and the market is soft.

analysis: A Fereghan Sarouk, 4'3" x 6'9", $800-1,200 -- a stray from the Day 2 rug consignment. Fereghan Sarouks are the earlier and finer Sarouk type, distinct from the American-market Sarouks of the 1920s, and a small one is a useful size. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Undated, like every other rug in this sale except 2268. The Fereghan attribution would matter if it were evidenced.

analysis: An Edwardian brass-bound oak standing bucket, $300-500. Catalogued to the period, so genuinely antique, and brass-bound oak peat and plate buckets are a handsome Anglo-Irish form that works as a wastepaper basket or a log bin without pretending to be anything else.
problems: These are reproduced heavily for the decorator trade and the reproductions use the same oak and the same brass. The tells are the coopering (period ones are true coopered staves with a chamfered base, reproductions are often ply or solid-turned), the brass thickness, and the liner. Missing or replaced liners are normal. Estimate is at the top of the market.

analysis: An antique Scottish Orkney armchair, $800-1,200. Orkney chairs -- driftwood or pine frames with hand-woven oat-straw hooded backs -- are a genuine and distinctive vernacular tradition, and the hooded ones are the desirable form. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. 'Antique' with no date: Orkney chairs have been made continuously since the 19th century and are still made by makers on the islands today, so age rests on the straw's condition, the frame timber and any maker's mark (Kirkness and Liberty-retailed examples are documented). Straw backs deteriorate and are replaced; a rewoven back is a large discount.
patience: Moderate. Orkney chairs appear occasionally in American sales and more often in Scotland.

analysis: A 19th-century view of Aonach Eagach in Glen Coe, $600-800. Catalogued to the century and specific about the place, which is more than most of the anonymous landscape material here manages. Victorian Scottish Highland views are competent, atmospheric and thoroughly out of fashion, which is what makes them affordable.
problems: No artist, so no maker premium and no criteria fit beyond age. At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for an anonymous Victorian landscape -- the market for these is $300-700 and falling. Read the frame separately: a period frame can be worth more than the picture.
patience: Very high. Victorian Highland landscapes are deep supply.

analysis: 'The House of Cards', OIL ON IVORY, unsigned, after the full-sized original by Jean-Baptiste-Simeon Chardin (1699-1779), in an original walnut bullseye panel frame with convex glass. The original bullseye frame is a genuinely good survival and the subject is a fine one. But 'after Chardin' means a copyist's picture by the standing principle, and the support is ivory. Federal ESA rules do allow a narrow de minimis exemption for a small, fixed, pre-1975 ivory component, and a painted wafer is a far better candidate for it than a solid carved figure -- but the exemption needs documentation of age and origin that this lot does not supply, and state law varies on top of it. Resale is recorded as zero on that basis, consistent with lot 2342. Paperwork could restore it; nothing in the catalogue is paperwork.
problems: Elephant ivory support, undocumented, resale zero. And 'after' does its usual work: this is a period copy of a Chardin, not a Chardin.

analysis: The description settles the material question against it: '16 white IVORY cut sticks with light background, hand painted with three women in Pompadour costume entertained by a gentleman playing a flute'. I had flagged this as the one fan in the Nichols consignment worth looking at precisely because it was described as painted rather than ivory. It is ivory. That puts it with 2338, 2392 and 2504 and the verdict has to change. There is genuine provenance here -- the fans come from the collection of Mary Eliot Nichols (1869-1966) of Danvers, Massachusetts, with this one tagged to Florence Ballou Nichols Lord (1907-1998) -- and that is real documented history, but provenance is not the same as the documentary proof of age that the ivory exemptions require.
problems: Elephant ivory sticks with no documentary proof of age. Resale is zero on the same basis as every other ivory lot in this sale: it cannot lawfully be sold on. This is a correction to my earlier call, which rested on the title's word 'painted' rather than on the description.

analysis: Same correction as 2340. The description reads: '(3) Engraved IVORY frames with small oval mirrors, all printed, depicting pastoral courtship scenes ... PLUS (2) on wood frames, also pastorals'. So three of the five are ivory and two are wood. The two wooden fans are unencumbered, but they are being sold as one lot with three that are not, and a lot containing ivory is a lot you cannot resell as offered. All five carry the Mary Eliot Nichols, Danvers provenance.
problems: Three of five fans are elephant ivory with no documentary proof of age, which takes the lot's resale to zero even though the two wooden fans are fine. Also note the ivory ones are described as 'all printed' rather than hand painted, so the decoration is the cheap grade regardless.

analysis: A mid-19th-century French ivory hand fan, Nichols family, $300-400. Catalogued to the period and genuinely antique, but elephant ivory with no documentation of age -- and the antique exemptions in federal and Maine law require documentary proof, which a family name does not supply.
problems: Ivory, undocumented. Resale is zero for the same reason as 2355, 2401 and 2489: whatever it is worth to look at, it cannot lawfully be sold on. One of eight ivory lots in this sale.
patience: Not applicable -- a category to avoid.

analysis: An early-19th-century Italian ivory hand fan, Nichols family, $250-350. Same conclusion as 2338.
problems: Ivory, undocumented, zero resale.

analysis: Three 19th-century Chinese ivory fans, Nichols family, $250-350. Chinese export carved ivory brise fans are extraordinary craft and this is three of them -- and all three are unsaleable for the same reason.
problems: Ivory, undocumented, zero resale.

analysis: An 18th-century French portrait miniature on ivory signed 'Catulle', $400-600. Genuinely antique by the catalogue's dating and portrait miniatures on ivory are a real field -- but the support is elephant ivory and the same restriction applies. There is a narrow federal de minimis exemption for objects containing small quantities of ivory, and a miniature's wafer might arguably qualify, but that requires documentation of age and origin the lot does not provide.
problems: Ivory support, undocumented; resale recorded as zero on that basis rather than on the painting's merits. 'Catulle' is also an unidentified signature -- the standing principle applies. Miniatures on ivory crack and warp with humidity.

analysis: A pair of 19th-century French Dieppe carved ivory figures, $400-600. Dieppe was the great French ivory-carving centre and its 19th-century figures are technically superb. Same conclusion.
problems: Ivory, undocumented, zero resale.

analysis: A 17th-century Italian ivory crucifix in a frame, $1,000-1,500. If the dating is right this would be one of the oldest objects in the sale. It is also elephant ivory, above the band, and subject to the same restriction.
problems: Ivory, undocumented, zero resale. Above budget at $1,320-1,980 all-in. Corpus figures of this type were also carved through the 19th century in the 17th-century manner.

analysis: A 19th-century Chinese ivory figure of a lady, $500-700. Same conclusion as every other ivory lot in this sale.
problems: Ivory, undocumented, zero resale.

analysis: A Chinese Qing ivory figure of an immortal, $500-700. Eighth and last of the ivory lots.
problems: Ivory, undocumented, zero resale. Worth noting the concentration: eight ivory lots across this sale, none with age documentation, all effectively unsaleable to a buyer who might one day want to let them go.

analysis: A pair of 19th-century Limoges polychrome enamel on metal candlesticks, $1,400-1,800 -- one of two identical lots (see 2350). Limoges painted enamel is a serious craft with a Renaissance lineage and the 19th-century revival pieces are well made. Above the band at $1,848-2,376 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Two identical pairs at identical estimates in the same session is unusual and suggests a decorative garniture split, or matched later production. Enamel on metal chips at every edge and the losses cannot be restored invisibly. No maker named -- Limoges is a place, and the 19th-century revival workshops signed their work.

analysis: A pair of 19th-century Limoges polychrome enamel candlesticks, $1,400-1,800 -- identical description and estimate to 2349. See that entry.
problems: Same as 2349, and competing with it directly.

analysis: A 17th-century altar figure of the Pieta, $1,500-2,500. Catalogued to the century, and Continental polychrome devotional sculpture of the period is genuine and moving work. Two to three times the band at $1,980-3,300 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Polychrome religious sculpture is almost always repainted at least once and the surviving original surface is what carries value -- the catalogue says nothing about it. Altar figures also raise the question of where they came from; church furnishings have their own provenance issues.

analysis: A pair of Italian gilded wood pricket candlesticks, $600-800 -- companion to the single 18th-century pricket at 2400. Carved and gilded altar prickets are a genuine Italian form and a pair is better than a single. At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band.
problems: No date on this pair, where 2400 gets an 18th-century attribution -- read the omission. Gilded wood is almost always regilded, and regilding is invisible in a photograph and halves the value. Prickets are also reproduced for the decorator trade in quantity.

analysis: An 18th-century Italian carved wood pricket candlestick, $300-400 -- and unlike its pair-lot neighbour 2387 this one carries a date. A single 18th-century carved altar pricket inside the band is a genuine antique at a fair price.
problems: A single rather than a pair, which halves the decorative appeal. Same regilding question as 2387: establish whether the gilt is original water gilding over gesso with genuine wear, or a later oil gilt. Carved wood of this age has usually been worm-damaged and repaired at the base.

analysis: A 16th-century walnut cassone with the Charles V Habsburg crest, $1,500-2,500. If right, this is among the oldest and most important objects in the sale -- a Renaissance marriage chest with an imperial armorial. Two to three times the band at $1,980-3,300 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Cassoni are also the single most reconstructed category in European furniture: genuine 16th-century carved panels are routinely mounted on later carcases, and complete 19th-century revival cassoni are common and convincing. An imperial crest is exactly the element most likely to have been added or recut. At this estimate the house is not claiming much confidence either.

analysis: A Renaissance plaque of the Black Madonna, southern France, $1,000-1,500. 'Renaissance' used as a period claim with no century and no material given. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. No material, no dimensions, no century within the Renaissance, no provenance. Devotional plaques in the medieval and Renaissance manner have been produced continuously since the 19th century for pilgrimage and decorative markets.

analysis: A Florentine relief stucco of the Madonna and Child, follower of Donatello (1386-1466), $20,000-30,000 -- the second-highest estimate in the sale after the Purdey pair. Quattrocento stucco Madonnas were cast in numbers from workshop moulds after Donatello, Rossellino and Ghiberti models, and genuine ones are museum objects. Twenty to thirty times the band.
problems: Massively above budget. 'Follower of' is a period-of-manufacture claim without an attribution, and these reliefs were also reproduced in the 19th century in exactly the same technique -- the Victorian and Berlin casts after quattrocento originals are numerous and have fooled museums. At this estimate the polychrome, the mould generation and the provenance all need expert examination and none is offered.

analysis: A 17th-century bird's-eye view of a Palm Sunday procession, $10,000-15,000 -- the highest-estimated painting in the sale. Topographical procession views of this date are genuine documentary pictures and the good ones are important. Ten to fifteen times the band.
problems: Massively above budget. No artist, no city, no support, no dimensions on a five-figure lot. At this level the picture needs a name or at least a firm school, and it has neither.

analysis: 'After Joshua Reynolds', $2,000-3,000. The standing principle is explicit: 'after [maker]' means copy or reproduction, not authenticity. This is a copy of a Reynolds by an unnamed hand at an unknown date, estimated at three to four times the band.
problems: Above budget for a copy. No date, no copyist, no dimensions, no support. Reynolds was the most copied English portraitist of the 18th and 19th centuries and the copies run from contemporary studio replicas to Victorian drawing-room decoration -- a range of twenty-fold in value, unaddressed here.
patience: Very high. There is a Reynolds copy in most English picture sales.

analysis: Harry Zeegers (Netherlands, 1929- ), $600-800. A living or recent Dutch painter with a thin auction record outside the Netherlands. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.
problems: Post-1926, no criteria fit. No date, no medium, no title, no dimensions. Continental artists with local followings do not price well in an American regional sale.

analysis: Felix Cohn (19th-20th c. Germany), $300-400. Straddles the antique line by the artist's own span, which means the picture could be either side of it. No auction record of note.
problems: No date, no medium, no title. The dates given are a lifespan bracket, not the work's date. Unindexed name.

analysis: A. Pictou, 'Visiting the Blacksmith', $1,000-2,000. An initial and a surname with no dates, no nationality and no auction record, estimated above the band at $1,320-2,640 all-in. Pictou is a Mi'kmaq surname and a Nova Scotia place name, which may or may not be relevant and the catalogue does not say.
problems: Above budget on an unindexed name. No date, no medium, no dimensions. The estimate has no visible basis.

analysis: A small Greco-Roman marble head on a museum plinth, $300-500. The plinth is doing rhetorical work -- a museum-style mount makes an object look accessioned. Nothing here is dated or provenanced.
problems: Unprovenanced classical antiquities carry real legal exposure: import restrictions, national patrimony claims and the practical impossibility of resale without documentation. Small marble heads in the antique manner are also produced in quantity in Italy and Egypt and aged convincingly. If genuine, the provenance problem; if not, the authenticity problem. Either way, no.

analysis: Two pieces of 'ancient Assyrian sandstone rubble', $400-600. This lot should be left alone, and the wording is why. Assyrian material means northern Iraq and Syria; both are subject to US import restrictions and UN sanctions specifically enacted because looted antiquities from those sites funded armed groups. 'Rubble' means architectural fragments broken out of a structure. No provenance, no export documentation and no collection history is offered.
problems: Unprovenanced Mesopotamian antiquities are the single clearest category to avoid in this sale. Resale is recorded as zero because lawful resale requires documentation that does not exist here, and possession itself can be a problem if the material is subject to a repatriation claim. Do not bid.

analysis: Ottoman gold-inlaid calligrapher's scissors, $600-800. Makta and calligrapher's scissors with gold koftgari inlay are genuine Ottoman craft objects, made for a specific and skilled use, and they are handsome as pure design. Part of the Ottoman consignment with the Iznik lots.
problems: No date. Koftgari and damascened steel is produced continuously in Turkey, Iran and India for the tourist trade and the modern work is good. Gold inlay on steel also lifts and is frequently restored. At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for something undated.

analysis: A 19th-century Persian Qajar helmet, $500-700. Catalogued to the century -- a kulah khud with its mail aventail, sliding nasal and plume holders is a striking object and Qajar arms and armour is a real field. At $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band.
problems: Qajar armour is the most reproduced category of Islamic arms: enormous quantities were made in Iran in the 19th and 20th centuries specifically for export and for the decorative trade, and 'revival' Qajar armour is close to indistinguishable from the working kind because both are chiselled steel by the same workshops. Damascened decoration is frequently later added. The catalogue's 19th-century dating is not evidence of manufacture for use.
patience: Very high. Qajar helmets are abundant.

analysis: Nine antique Asian opium pipes, $600-800. Opium paraphernalia is a documented and collected field -- the bamboo stems, the ceramic bowls, the silver and paktong fittings are real craft objects and the good ones are 19th century.
problems: 'Antique' with no date. Opium pipes are also faked in quantity for the Western market, and made-up pipes assembled from mismatched parts are the norm rather than the exception. Nine of them means nine sets of that question. Some antique pipes have ivory or tortoiseshell mounts, which would raise the restrictions covered elsewhere. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.

analysis: A 17th-century Chinese Buddha with two children, $1,000-1,500. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in, and the century attribution has nothing behind it in the catalogue.
problems: Above budget. No material, no dimensions, no provenance. Chinese religious sculpture is reproduced continuously and the archaistic ones are aged convincingly. Religious sculpture provenance questions apply.

analysis: A finely carved Chinese hardwood bird cage with accessories, $500-700. Chinese bird cages are genuine craft objects -- turned bamboo or hardwood, carved hooks, and fitted porcelain feeders and water cups, which is what 'accessories' should mean. The accessories are frequently the best part; period cups can be small pieces of good porcelain in their own right.
problems: No date. Cages are made continuously and the decorative ones are numerous. The accessories need counting and assessing individually -- a cage with its original matched porcelain set is a different object from a cage with three modern cups. At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band.

analysis: A vintage Chinese boxed souvenir collection, $300-500. The word souvenir is the whole assessment.
problems: No date, no contents listed. Souvenir goods have no collector market. Estimate is several times the value.

analysis: Three Tibetan saddle rugs, $500-700. Tibetan saddle rugs -- the shaped makden and the rectangular under-saddle -- are a genuine and distinctive weaving tradition with a small collecting field. Undated.
problems: No date. Modern Nepali production copies these forms for the decorative market. Saddle rugs are used objects and are usually worn through in the centre. At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for undated pieces.

analysis: A large Tibetan cloisonne two-part stupa, $3,500-4,500. A substantial and impressive object. Four to six times the band at $4,620-5,940 all-in.
problems: Massively above budget. No date. Large cloisonne stupas are produced in Nepal and China for the devotional and decorative markets today. Religious object provenance questions apply.

analysis: William M. Hall (19th c. Maine), $800-1,200. A 19th-century Maine painter is the rare lot that hits both the age criterion and the Maine criterion at once, which almost nothing in the Maine section does -- the brief notes that the Monhegan and Ogunquit material almost never clears a hundred years. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. No dates for the artist beyond the century, no auction record of substance, no medium, no title, no dimensions. The estimate assumes a market the name does not obviously have. If it stalls under $800 in the room it becomes worth a second look purely on the double criteria fit.
patience: Moderate. Nineteenth-century Maine painters other than the famous few come up irregularly.

analysis: Ira W. Hamilton (early 20th c. Maine), $600-800 -- one of the very few Maine artists in this sale whose working period actually straddles the 1926 line rather than sitting decades after it. That makes it more interesting than the contemporary Maine material, which earns its place on regional desirability alone.
problems: At $792-1,056 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band. 'Early 20th c.' is a bracket, not a date, and the work could be either side of 1926. Hamilton has a thin auction record. No medium, no title, no dimensions, no subject.
patience: High. Minor Maine painters run constantly at Thomaston.

analysis: Anne-Emmanuelle Marpeau (France/Maine, contemporary), $2,000-2,500. A living artist working in Maine; the Maine criterion applies on regional desirability rather than age. Three times the band at $2,640-3,300 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Catalogued as contemporary, so no age criterion. Living-artist work at auction typically resells below the artist's own prices, and $2,000-2,500 is a gallery number.

analysis: Attributed to William Bradford, $3,000-5,000. Bradford was the New Bedford marine and Arctic painter, a genuinely significant American artist, and a real Bradford is a five- to six-figure picture. 'Attributed to' at $3,000-5,000 is the house saying it thinks the picture is probably right but will not warrant it. Four to six times the band.
problems: Above budget. 'Attributed to' with no supporting provenance is an opinion. Bradford is also extensively copied and misattributed -- Arctic and New England coastal scenes in his manner were painted by contemporaries and by later imitators. At this estimate you are paying a substantial fraction of a real Bradford for an unwarranted one.

analysis: An Omersa for Abercrombie & Fitch rhino ottoman, $1,000-1,500 -- one of two Omersa lots (see 3003). Dimitri Omersa's leather animals, made in Britain and retailed by Abercrombie & Fitch from the 1960s, are a genuinely collected mid-century design object with an active market and real charm. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Omersa animals are still in production today under the Omersa & Company name, so 'vintage' matters and the tells are the label, the stitching and the hide's patina. Leather dries and splits at the seams; restuffing and reseaming is expensive. Post-1926 by decades.
patience: Moderate. Omersa animals appear regularly in design sales.

analysis: A Dimitri Omersa UK leather pig ottoman, $700-900. Companion to 3001 and the cheaper of the two; the pig is one of the standard Omersa forms. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band.
problems: Above budget. Same production-date question as 3001 -- these are still made. Same leather condition exposure.

analysis: A 19th-century carved and painted wood Pegasus, $2,000-3,000. Catalogued to the century, and a large carved and painted mythological figure -- from a carousel, a shop sign or an architectural setting -- is exactly the Day 3 folk material this sale is built around. Three to four times the band.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Same objection as the rest of the Day 3 trade-sign and carving consignment: no maker, no origin, no function stated, and this is the most reproduced category in American folk art. The 19th-century dating is the house's claim and nothing supports it in the catalogue.

analysis: A large Powers Irish Whiskey bar-back panel, $2,000-3,000 -- companion to the Powers pub sign at 3026 and the Guinness panel at 3031. Three Irish pub-fitting lots in one consignment. Three to four times the band.
problems: Above budget. Irish pub fittings are manufactured for the theme-pub trade on an industrial scale and have been since the 1970s; a genuine Victorian bar-back panel is documented and rare, and nothing here claims a date. Three of them in one sale is itself a signal.

analysis: A Guinness painted wood presentation panel, 7'11", $800-1,200. Third of the Irish pub-fitting group. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in and nearly eight feet long.
problems: Above budget, undated, and eight feet of painted wood is a siting problem. Guinness advertising is among the most reproduced brand material there is.

analysis: A Harriet Whitney Frishmuth speed car mascot cast by Gorham, $3,000-5,000. Frishmuth was a significant American sculptor and Gorham was her founder; her radiator mascots of the 1920s are documented, signed, and genuinely collected. This is the best-attributed sculpture in the sale -- named artist, named foundry, dateable form. It straddles the 1926 line and is four to six times the band.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Frishmuth mascots are also recast -- later and unauthorised casts exist -- so the signature, the Gorham mark, the casting quality and the patina all need examination. Mascots were mounted on cars and used; expect base wear and possible replating.
patience: Low. Frishmuth mascots are genuinely scarce -- a real regret at this budget.

analysis: A large cast stone torso of a woman, $400-600 -- one of two cast stone torsos (see 3044). Cast stone is a reproduction medium; garden sculpture of this type is produced continuously.
problems: No artist, no date. Two nearly identical lots in one session. Estimate is above the garden-ornament market.

analysis: A small cast stone nude torso of a woman, $300-400. Companion to 3042.
problems: Same as 3042.

analysis: A Salterini 'Radar' iron tete-a-tete bistro set, $500-700. John Salterini's wrought-iron furniture is genuine mid-century American design with a collecting following, and the Radar pattern is one of the recognised ones. Post-1926 and at $660-924 all-in it is at the top of the band.
problems: At the band ceiling. Salterini is widely copied and unmarked pieces are attributed to him freely; look for the label or the tag. Wrought iron rusts from the inside of the tube and repainting hides it. No criteria fit.
patience: Moderate. Salterini appears regularly in design sales.

analysis: A five-piece vintage wrought iron dining set, $800-1,200. Anonymous mid-century patio furniture. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget for unattributed garden furniture. No maker, no date. Compare 3043, which at least has a name.

analysis: A five-piece bamboo patio dining set, 'Boothbay style in butter enamel paint', $600-800. 'Boothbay style' is a decorator's phrase rather than an attribution, though it does gesture at the midcoast. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.
problems: No maker, no date. Painted bamboo furniture is fragile -- the joints let go and the paint chips. 'Style' with a Maine place name attached is marketing.

analysis: A replica Tutankhamun throne, $3,000-4,000. The catalogue says replica, which is honest and settles the question. Egyptian Museum-authorised and unauthorised replicas of the throne were made in numbers, particularly around the 1970s touring exhibitions.
problems: Above budget by four to five times, for an object the house has told you is a copy. No date, no maker, no dimensions.

analysis: A circa 1900 golden oak American tallcase clock with chimes, $3,000-5,000. Catalogued to c.1900, so genuinely antique, and a chiming tallcase clock is a serious piece of American cabinet and horological work. Four to six times the band.
problems: Above budget. Tallcase clocks are also the furniture category where movements and cases are most often married; establish that the movement is original to the case and that the chime train works. Golden oak cases specifically are a turn-of-the-century mass-market product rather than a cabinetmaker's, so the value is in the movement. No maker named.

analysis: A miniature Russian icon of Alexander Nevsky, $300-500. Small travelling and personal icons are a genuine tradition and 19th-century ones are plentiful enough to be affordable. Inside the band.
problems: No date at all. Russian icons are the most systematically faked category of religious art in the market -- aged panels, artificially darkened varnish and modern painting over old boards are routine, and a miniature is the easiest size to fake. Check the panel's construction (period ones have inset battens and a carved kovcheg recess), the gesso, and whether the craquelure runs through the paint or has been drawn on. Also confirm it left Russia lawfully; cultural-property export from Russia is restricted.

analysis: A pair of Yudin Russian brass Sabbath candlesticks, $800-1,200. Yudin was a documented Warsaw-area brass foundry producing Judaica in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and marked Yudin Sabbath candlesticks are a real category with a specific collecting audience. Named maker and genuinely antique. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. The maker's mark should be struck on the base -- confirm it is there and legible, because unmarked brass candlesticks of the same pattern are worth a fraction. Brass Sabbath candlesticks are also reproduced. No date given.
patience: Moderate. Marked Yudin pairs appear a few times a year in Judaica sales.

analysis: A pair of 19th-century John Jelliff carved walnut armchairs, $600-800. Jelliff of Newark was one of the best American Renaissance Revival cabinetmakers and his carved figural heads are a recognisable signature -- this is a documented American maker, which is more than most furniture in this sale offers. Catalogued to the century.
problems: Upholstered Victorian seating in the weakest furniture market there is; Jelliff's name lifts it but does not rescue it. Attribution to Jelliff is also made freely on any carved Renaissance Revival chair -- the real ones have specific carved masks and specific proportions. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band, and reupholstery on a pair would cost as much again.
patience: High. Renaissance Revival seating is abundant and cheap; Jelliff-attributed pairs less so.

analysis: J. Chester (Skip) Armstrong (Oregon), $20,000-30,000 -- tied with the Donatello-follower stucco as the second-highest estimate in the sale. Armstrong is a documented contemporary Oregon woodcarver whose large sculptures do reach these levels. Twenty to thirty times the band.
problems: Massively above budget. Contemporary, wrong coast, no criteria fit. No title, medium or dimensions given on a five-figure lot.

analysis: A 'Hepplewhite style' inlaid mahogany server, $1,000-1,500. 'Style' means the cataloguer is declining to commit to a period, and on Hepplewhite that means Colonial Revival -- these were made in quantity from about 1900 to 1960. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget for revival furniture in a collapsed market. 'Style' with no date. Brown furniture of this kind regularly fails to sell.

analysis: A W. Kohler mesquite floor lamp with a pierced copper shade, $500-700. Studio craft lighting in the Arts and Crafts idiom -- mesquite is a southwestern wood, so this is contemporary American studio work rather than anything period.
problems: Unindexed maker, no date. Nouveau- and Craftsman-style studio lighting is made continuously and resells poorly. At $660-924 all-in the estimate is at the top of the band for contemporary craft.

analysis: Jamali (India/NY/FL, 1944- ), $2,500-3,500 -- one of two Jamali lots (see 3274). Jamali is a living artist with a substantial gallery operation and a promotional apparatus; his auction results are considerably below his gallery prices, which is the usual pattern for artists sold primarily through their own galleries. Three to four times the band.
problems: Above budget. Contemporary, no criteria fit. The gap between gallery price and auction result on this artist is large and the estimate appears to be set from the former.

analysis: Jamali (India/NY/FL, 1944- ), $600-800 -- the cheaper of the two Jamali lots. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.
problems: Same as 3273 and competing with it. Contemporary, no criteria fit.

analysis: Paul Maddrell (Maine, 1948- ), $800-1,200. A living Maine artist; the Maine criterion applies on regional desirability rather than age. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Contemporary. No medium, title or dimensions. Thin auction record.

analysis: John Bisbee (American/Maine, b. 1965), 'Leaf', $3,000-4,500. Bisbee is the most seriously established contemporary artist in this sale -- a Brunswick-based sculptor working exclusively in twelve-inch bright common nails, with museum exhibitions and a genuine national reputation. The Maine connection is real and so is the market. Four to six times the band.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Contemporary, so no age criterion. No dimensions given, which on a Bisbee matters enormously -- his work runs from small wall pieces to room-filling installations.
patience: Moderate. Bisbee's work appears occasionally at auction; most of it moves through galleries.

analysis: Tim Nguyen (20th-21st c. Honolulu), $400-600 -- the cheapest of three Nguyen lots (3297, 3298, 3299) with estimates running from $400 to $7,000. That spread across three works by one unindexed artist in one sale is worth noting: it means the house is pricing by size or by impression rather than by any market record.
problems: Unindexed name, no date, no medium, no title. Honolulu, so no regional fit. Three lots by the same artist competing.

analysis: Tim Nguyen (20th-21st c. Honolulu), $5,000-7,000 -- the highest of the three Nguyen lots and, at $6,600-9,240 all-in, seven to nine times the band. An artist with no established auction record carrying a five-figure all-in cost.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin on an unindexed name. No date, no medium, no title, no dimensions. Nothing in the catalogue supports the step up from 3297's $400.

analysis: Tim Nguyen (20th-21st c. Honolulu), $1,000-1,500. Third Nguyen lot. Above the band.
problems: Same as 3297 and 3298.

analysis: Two Patrick Young (American) 'Janet Series' hand-painted photographs, $800-1,200. Hand-painted photographs are a genuine technique and a named series suggests a body of work, but the artist does not index. Above the band at $1,056-1,584 all-in.
problems: Above budget. No date, no edition, no dimensions. Contemporary photography bought at auction resells poorly unless the name carries.

analysis: Mark Harrington (Franklin, Maine), $2,000-2,500. A Maine artist with a regional following; the Maine criterion applies on desirability rather than age. Three times the band at $2,640-3,300 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Contemporary. No medium, title or dimensions. Maine artist prices are made in Maine, which means this room is where they are highest.

analysis: Dan Miller (Winter Harbor, Maine), $700-900. A Downeast Maine artist. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band.
problems: Above budget. Contemporary, thin record, no medium or title given.
patience: Very high. Contemporary Maine painters are the deepest supply in this sale.

analysis: Cynthia Goodman Brantley (20th c. NY), $1,000-1,500 -- one of two identical lots (see 3320). An unindexed New York artist with two works at identical estimates in the same session. Above the band.
problems: Above budget on an unindexed name. No date, no medium, no title. Two lots competing.

analysis: Cynthia Goodman Brantley (20th c. NY), $1,000-1,500 -- identical to 3319.
problems: Same as 3319.

analysis: A Caplan mid-century railyard scene, $700-900 -- second of three Caplan lots (1348, 3322, 3323). A surname-only signature with no first name, no dates and no auction record. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band.
problems: Above budget on an unidentified signature. Three lots by the same hand in one sale suggests a single consignment rather than a market.

analysis: 'Caplan, 51' mid-century market scene, $700-900 -- third Caplan lot and the only one with a date, taken from the signature itself. 1951, so firmly modern.
problems: Same as 3322. Above the band at $924-1,188 all-in on an unidentified signature.

analysis: Marjorie Moore (Casco Bay, ME, 1944- ), $700-900 -- companion to 1459. A living Maine artist, Casco Bay subject. At $924-1,188 all-in it is above the band.
problems: Above budget. Contemporary. Two Moore lots competing in one sale. No medium, title or dimensions.

analysis: Otty Merrill (Tenants Harbor, ME / NYC), $300-400. Tenants Harbor is fifteen minutes from Thomaston, which makes this hyper-local material -- the brief notes that named-midcoast-town work sells to a small but committed regional audience. Inside the band, which most of the Maine artist lots are not.
problems: Thin auction record, no date, no medium, no title, no subject. Modern, so nothing on the age criterion; it earns its place on regional desirability alone and that should be said explicitly. Hyper-local also means the resale audience is small.
patience: Very high. Contemporary and modern Maine painters run constantly at Thomaston.

analysis: Jan Ehrenworth (20th-21st c. MA), $300-500. A Massachusetts artist with no auction record. No date, medium, title or dimensions.
problems: Unindexed name, no information. Wrong state for the regional criterion.

analysis: W. Anthony Evanko (Colombia/NY/NM, 1953- ), $300-400. A living artist with a thin record, no Maine connection and no information beyond the name.
problems: Unindexed, no date, no medium, no title. No criteria fit.

analysis: David Slee (American, b. 1947), reclining nude, $600-800. A living artist with a modest record. At $792-1,056 all-in it is at the top of the band.
problems: Contemporary, no criteria fit, no medium or dimensions. Estimate at the band ceiling for an artist with no established market.

analysis: Ragna Bruno-Torkanowsky (20th c. Maine), $1,000-1,500. A Maine artist; the Maine criterion applies on regional desirability. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. No date, no medium, no title. Thin auction record.

analysis: John S. Caggiano (NY 1949- ), 'Fish Beach', $1,000-1,500. Caggiano is a Gloucester-based painter with a real regional following in Massachusetts, and 'Fish Beach' is a Monhegan place name -- so this may well be a Maine subject by a Cape Ann painter. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget. Contemporary. Caggiano's market is Gloucester rather than Maine, though a Monhegan subject bridges the two. No medium or dimensions.

analysis: Nancy J. Hill (Prospect Harbor, ME), $250-350 -- the cheapest Maine artist lot in this group and inside the band with room. Prospect Harbor is Downeast, which is hyper-local in the way the brief describes: a small, committed regional audience.
problems: No auction record, no date, no medium, no title, no dimensions. Modern, so it earns its place on regional desirability alone and not on age -- worth saying plainly. Resale would be limited to the same small regional audience.

analysis: Jill Hoy (late 20th - early 21st c. Maine), $4,000-5,000. Hoy is a Stonington painter with a genuine and active market -- one of the better-established contemporary Maine names, and her bright coastal landscapes sell well in-state. Five to six times the band.
problems: Above budget by a wide margin. Contemporary, so nothing on the age criterion. Her prices are made in Maine galleries and a Maine saleroom is where they hold up best, not where they are cheap.
patience: Moderate. Hoy paintings appear regularly in Maine sales.

analysis: William J. Maloney (MA 1932- ), $1,000-1,500. A Massachusetts artist with a thin record. Above the band at $1,320-1,980 all-in.
problems: Above budget, unindexed, no date, no medium, no title. Wrong state for the regional criterion.

analysis: Molly Pitkin (Newcastle, ME), $400-600 -- Newcastle is on the Damariscotta River, twenty minutes from Bath, so this is about as local as the Maine material gets. Inside the band at $528-792 all-in. The last lot in this analysis, and a fair representative of the whole Maine section: a real regional artist, a real regional audience, and no age claim of any kind.
problems: No auction record, no date, no medium, no title, no dimensions. Modern, so it earns its place on regional desirability rather than age -- which the brief asks to be said explicitly, and this is the case where it matters most. Estimate is at the top of what unlisted Maine painters make.
